The lands of men are held together in a loose alliance. Stories of old tell of cyclical cataclysms when demons from the earth emerge to devour the inhabitants of villages, towns, and cities.1. Ideally the vast majority of society would only look at these tales as rumor, superstition, and hearsay2. The wakening would start in remote areas as the creatures are weak from their extended slumber. As the creatures regain strength they start to breed3 and the events begin to snowball.

It is important that the creatures remain shrouded in secrecy. If possible a special resistance or unique feature should be added to help induce panic4. When the players are first called to an incident portray the scene in such a way that it fits the previous mold (mundane masked as sinister)5. As the players investigate give them a false trail and during the climax of the false trail have the monster make its first appearance6.

After the party's return the events become more frequent. The delay between attacks increased, and the brutality rises. The creatures no longer confine their slaughter to hunting and feeding, they now kill for pleasure. If the players are keeping track of attacks on a map the map should start getting filled. The players, guards, and military forces can no longer protect the isolated communities. Those who can make it to larger settlements do so.

When the party starts facing the creatures they should be easily handled. The creatures, however, should level up faster than the players and their actions should transition from curious to cruel. As time continues the players will need to carefully choose where and when the fight.

This is not a war to exterminate the awakened hellspawn, but to survive until they retire to their slumber7.

Notes

  1. To make this more of an issue you can choose to have them target users of magic, or whatever the driving force in your world is. In a society built around magic the loss of users to improve crop yields, mend broken dams, heal the sick, etc. would plunge the world into a dark age.

  2. Consider starting the campaign with several similar mythos and perhaps have the new characters participate in a few wild goose chases. Masking the mundane as something sinister ("Werewolves" are raiders dressed in furs, "Vampires" are a cultists who wrongly believe blood will grant immortality, etc.) should desensitize the group and cause hesitation in believing the old folk tales.

  3. Think X-COM or a locust infestation.

  4. Perhaps they are healed with magic, have wounds that cannot be healed due to a corrosive saliva, their wounds plant embryos in the victim, or the corpses bloat up and resemble plague victims. Hell add some mind control or shape shifting abilities.

  5. A merchant noticed the mining town was deserted and bloody drag marks led into the forest. The merchant assumed raiders were caught up in a bloodlust.

  6. The party tracks a known band of thieves and robbers to their den ten miles from the town. They engage the bandits and after a lengthy fight dispatch the last of the criminal scum. At this point the party is wounded, low on supplies, and exhausted. One of the party members, spots a creature watching them from the forest. Roll secret spot checks for the players and assign the true siting to either the highest spot check or the most gullible player. Another player or two may have seen something but will surely believe it to be a wild animal or escaped fugitive.

  7. Hopefully a crazy scholar or overly curious youth will have some knowledge about these myths.

I'm just looking for something incredibly basic. I always was interested in Geopolitics, I'm not looking for a specific region or time period on Earth, but perhaps maybe the British Empire or Ancient China. Like I said though I'm looking for a book introduction to the world of Geopolitics. Thanks in advance. :)
What are recommended Geopolitical books that anybody interested in Politics/geopol must read?

I would highly recommend Robert Massie's Dreadnought. It's focus is the naval arms race leading up to WW1, but where it shines is illustrating the personalities that led to the conflict. He's a great writer who can captivate even a non historian. It's part of the reason why it's not a beloved book by many historians. (Th other reason is that in the past few decades the study of history tends to discount the impact individuals have on shaping events. I understand both positions, but I suspect the truth lies in the middle).
Empire by Niall Ferguson is a highly readable account of the British Empire. Also check out his War of the World.
